else.text: Dot Tallis. This is my yard, those are my animals, and that's my clipboard. Wipe your feet or don't, but don't touch the clipboard.
I keep the old breeds, the ones the supermarkets stopped asking for. If nobody keeps them they're gone in a generation, and no amount of sorry brings a breed back.

Here's how it works. Two of yours that like you, Fond or better, a male and a female of the same kind, or a cross I've got in the book. I put them together. One pair a day. And I won't have close kin. Not on my farm.
Then you walk. A basket takes a few thousand steps, and more out of season: spring for the furry and the feathered, summer for the scaly. The heat lamp isn't free either, and I charge for it.
Come back when you've walked it off and I'll hand them over. Nobody buys or sells them here. I keep animals, I don't sell them.

then.text: Hirta's flock is in good order, and so is mine. Go and see something that isn't a sheep.
Four lambs, three different families. That's a flock, not a household. The society's grant is in your hand and I won't hear a word about it.
And now you know why the Hirta sheep ride out a bad winter and a small flock of cousins doesn't. Dr Keir will want to hear.

else.text: Have you been to see Dr Keir yet? Roslin, outside Edinburgh. She'll tell you why a flock needs founders. I only know it from the animals.

Soay sheep. St Kilda, out past the Hebrides. When the last islanders left in 1930 they put about a hundred of them on Hirta in 1932 and left them to it. They've been counted every year since the eighties, and the numbers swing wildly: up, then a hard winter, then down.
I can't hand you a Soay, they stay where they are. But a Loaghtan is the same sort of animal, a small hardy primitive island sheep, so we'll do it with those.
Raise four lambs of your own, and not all from the one pair. A flock isn't a family. Three different pairings, and I'll count no more than two from any one.
Then go and ask Dr Keir at the Roslin Institute, outside Edinburgh, why I'm being so fussy. Come back when you've got your four.

then.text: Bríd's herd is thriving. She sent a photograph. Four black cows in the rain and not one of them looked pleased. It's perfect.
Four young ones, from pairs with no parent in common. Not a cousin in the lot, as far as the book says. I'll send them over to Bríd on the Kerry yard.
Grant's yours. Tell Dr Keir. She'll have another list; she always has another list.

else.text: Dr Keir at Roslin will tell you how to tell cousins from strangers. I do it by looking at the way they stand, which is why I need her.
Kerry cattle. Small and black and hardy, bred for hill grass in the south-west of Ireland, and one of the oldest dairy breeds in Europe. The Dexter was made from them. They've been rare a long time.
My cousin Bríd has a sister yard in Kerry and wants a herd that isn't one family. The Moolet is the nearest thing we've got to a Dexter, so we'll use those.

Four young Moolets, from at least two pairings with no parent in common. Dr Keir can tell you how to read a pedigree. Mind it's a long game: it's no good if you pair siblings back together, because I'll refuse.
Another list? One at a time. Finish the flock for Hirta first. Then we'll talk Kerry.

breed_loaghtan.text: Four horns, mouse-brown fleece and the long, level stare of an animal that has outlived several governments. It belongs to the Isle of Man, and it's one of the primitive short-tailed sheep, like the Soay.
Dot says a small flock needs careful pairing to keep what variety it has, and the Loaghtan is the proof. Don't ask the Loaghtan. The Loaghtan has opinions.

breed_herdwick.text: A Herdwick, from the Lake District fells. Grey-faced and sturdy, and the lambs are born dark and fade to grey as they grow up.
Beatrix Potter kept Herdwicks, and left her fell farms to the National Trust in 1943, with their flocks. They are the reason a lot of Lakeland still looks the way it does.

breed_dextera.text: A Dexter: one of the smallest cattle breeds in the world, from the south-west of Ireland, and descended from the Kerry.

It's a short-legged breed, and the shortness comes from a single gene. One copy gives the short legs of a Dexter. Two copies is a calf that doesn't survive, which is why breeders pay such close attention to pairings. A good lesson, if a sad one.

breed_donkey.text: Dot keeps a donkey because nobody else will. Her view is that a donkey is the most sensible animal on the farm, and the only one that has never been wrong.

A donkey and a horse can have a mule, which is strong and clever and has no foals of its own. The horse has 64 chromosomes and the donkey 62, so a mule has 63, and 63 won't pair up. Dr Keir will tell you more.

breed_visitor.text: I came for the lambs and stayed for the clipboard. She asked my name and then wrote it down, and now I'm on a list.
Don't ask for a pair Dot doesn't approve of. She will look at you. It is worse than being shouted at.
